subject: Beta-binomial w/poisson count of unknown total - working around int constraint?

messages.author: eef3651eaaf833d9
messages.subject: Beta-binomial w/poisson count of unknown total - working around int constraint?
parts:
Hi all, 

Thanks for the great language and for everyone's contribution to this mailing list,

Hopefully this question is general enough to be of interest to more than my specific problem:


I'm trying to fit a Beta-Binomial model where the "true" N # of possible observations is considered an unknown mixture of data observations and missing counts, i.e. 

where y is # of successes in n trials, 


Y ~ BetaBinomial(N, alpha, beta)

N = Nobs + Nmiss

Nmiss ~ Poisson(lambda)

and etc. for the usual priors and additive link functions. 


Marginalizing isn't terribly helpful in this situation, as the beta-binomial is constrained to require an 'int' input, and even if I were to marginalize the Poisson to a conjugate gamma posterior, I would lose in the 'Nobs + Nmiss' term. 

Any ideas on how to work around this in Stan would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks,
Graeme

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Beta-binomial w/poisson count of unknown total - working around int constraint?
parts:
There's no general way to marginalize out count variables in
Stan.

What does the rest of the model look like and is there
a reasonable upper and lower bound on Nmiss? Sometimes
you can do continuous approximations (not by rounding, but
by considering Y to be continuous) and sometimes you can
marginalize out if the reasonable range for Nmiss is constrained
to the hundreds.

- Bob

messages.author: eef3651eaaf833d9
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Beta-binomial w/poisson count of unknown total - working around int constraint?
parts:
Thanks for the input, I'll look into approximations using Y as cont - the bounds of Nmiss are quite small, somewhere from 0 - 10. 

Current model code:

data{
    int<lower=1> N;
    int plantB[N];
    int Nobs[N];
}
parameters{
    real a;
    real<lower=0> theta;
}
model{
    vector[N] pbar;
    int n[N];
    theta ~ exponential( 1 );
    a ~ normal( 0 , 2 );
    for ( i in 1:N ) {
        pbar[i] = a; // Plus other covariate predictors in the full model
        pbar[i] = inv_logit(pbar[i]);
    }
    plantB ~ beta_binomial( Nobs , pbar*theta , (1-pbar)*theta );
}


Preferably it would be something like

data{
    int<lower=1> N;
    int plantB[N];
    int Nobs[N];
}
parameters{
    real a;
    real<lower=0> theta;
    int Nmiss[N]
}
model{
    vector[N] pbar;
    int n[N];
    theta ~ exponential( 1 );
    lambda ~ gamma( 0.001, 0.001); //or some better prior
    a ~ normal( 0 , 2 );
    
    for ( i in 1:N ) {
        pbar[i] = a;     // Plus other covariate predictors in the full model
        pbar[i] = inv_logit(pbar[i]);
    }
    Nmiss ~ poisson(lambda);
    plantB ~ beta_binomial( Nobs + Nmiss, pbar*theta , (1-pbar)*theta );
}

Thanks again for the help,

Best,
Graeme

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Beta-binomial w/poisson count of unknown total - working around int constraint?
parts:
If it's in the 0--10 range, you can marginalize over 0--50 and it'll
probably still be efficient enough and provide close to the same answer.

> Nmiss ~ poisson(lambda);
> plantB ~ beta_binomial( Nobs + Nmiss, pbar*theta , (1-pbar)*theta );

So what you'd get is this:

{
real lp[51];
for (n in 1:N)
for (n_miss in 0:50) {
lp[n_miss + 1] = poisson_lpmf(n_miss | lambda)
+ beta_binomial_lpmf(plantB[n] | Nobs[n] + n_miss, ...);
target += log_sum_exp(lp);
}
}

The awkard indexing is because 1 is the smallest integer, but we
have to consider n_miss = 0.

If you want a probability distribution over the posterior for n_miss,
you can use this:

log_p_n_miss = lp - log_sum_exp(lp);

but you'll have to do it for each n. Then you have:

log_p_n_miss[k] = log Pr[n_miss = k - 1 | y]

where y is all your observed data.

- Bob

On Tue, May 2, 2017 at 6:19 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
1.  You can perhaps approx that sum of 51 terms by an integral that can be evaluated in closed form.
2.  To channel Andrew, don't do the gamma(.001, .001).
A

On May 2, 2017, at 9:17 PM, Graeme Baird <grm...@gmail.com> wrote:

Brilliant! Thanks for the help, Bob. 

For the record, here's the code I managed to get running:

data{
  int N;
  int plantB[N];
  int total[N];
}

parameters{
  real a;
  real<lower=0> theta;
  real<lower=0> lambda;
}

model{
  vector[N] pbar;
  real lp[51];

  lambda ~ gamma( 0.001, 0.001);
  theta ~ exponential( 1 );
  a ~ normal (0,1);

  for (n in 1:N){
    pbar[n] = a;     // Plus other covariate predictors in the full model
    pbar[n] = inv_logit(pbar[n]);
    for (n_miss in 0:50) {
      lp[n_miss + 1] = poisson_lpmf(n_miss | lambda)
      + beta_binomial_lpmf(plantB[n] | total[n] + n_miss, pbar[n]*theta , (1-pbar[n])*theta);
      }
    target += log_sum_exp(lp);
  }
}

Runs like molasses, though, will have to think about how to vectorize the main for loop...

GB


On Mon, Apr 17, 2017 at 11:38 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
If it's in the 0--10 range, you can marginalize over 0--50 and it'll
probably still be efficient enough and provide close to the same answer.

> Nmiss ~ poisson(lambda);
> plantB ~ beta_binomial( Nobs + Nmiss, pbar*theta , (1-pbar)*theta );


So what you'd get is this:

{
  real lp[51];
  for (n in 1:N)
    for (n_miss in 0:50) {
      lp[n_miss + 1] = poisson_lpmf(n_miss | lambda)
                     + beta_binomial_lpmf(plantB[n] | Nobs[n] + n_miss, ...);
      target += log_sum_exp(lp);
  }
}

The awkard indexing is because 1 is the smallest integer, but we
have to consider n_miss = 0.

If you want a probability distribution over the posterior for n_miss,
you can use this:

  log_p_n_miss = lp - log_sum_exp(lp);

but you'll have to do it for each n.  Then you have:

  log_p_n_miss[k] = log Pr[n_miss = k - 1 | y]

where y is all your observed data.

- Bob
